nameStory: The 'cut-leaved' part of this plant's name comes from its deeply divided leaves that look like they've been cut with tiny scissors into delicate, lacy segments. The 'crane's-bill' name refers to the long, pointed seed pods that stick straight up like a crane's beak - when the seeds are ripe, these 'beaks' split open and spring back to fling the seeds away from the parent plant.
description: Cut-leaved crane's-bill is a small, sprawling annual herb originally from Europe that has made itself at home in some parts of North America. This delicate-looking plant grows low to the ground, typically reaching only 6-12 inches tall, with stems that tend to spread outward rather than grow straight up. Its most distinctive features are its deeply cut, feathery leaves and small pink or purple flowers, followed by the characteristic long, pointed seed pods that give all crane's-bills their name.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are deeply cut into 5-7 narrow, finger-like segments that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, creating a delicate, lacy appearance that looks almost fern-like

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to purple flowers with 5 rounded petals, each about 1/4 inch across, often appearing in pairs and having a sweet, mild fragrance

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The distinctive 'crane's bill' seed pods are long, straight, and pointed, standing upright like tiny spears before explosively splitting to scatter seeds

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing and spreading, with stems that branch and sprawl along the ground rather than standing upright, creating small patches

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, somewhat weak stems that feel slightly sticky when touched and are often reddish-tinged, especially at the joints where leaves attach

habitat: Cut-leaved crane's-bill is extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation, likely found in disturbed soils, garden edges, or waste places where European plants sometimes establish. When present, it typically grows in sandy or well-drained soils in sunny to partially shaded locations, often among other weedy or introduced species.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge early with their characteristic deeply-cut leaves appearing first, followed by the start of flowering in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering and fruiting period, when the small pink flowers and distinctive crane's-bill seed pods are most visible and diagnostic.
seasonality.fall: Seeds have been dispersed and plants begin to decline, with dried stems and seed pod remnants sometimes persisting into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Annual plant dies back completely, leaving no above-ground traces until seeds germinate the following spring.

funFact: Cut-leaved crane's-bill has an unexpected superpower in the gardening world - extracts from this humble little weed can actually boost the germination rates of hemp seeds, though scientists are still figuring out exactly how this botanical friendship works!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small crane's-bills like Carolina crane's-bill or small-flowered crane's-bill, but cut-leaved crane's-bill has much more deeply divided, feathery leaves - think of the difference between a regular hand and one wearing lacy gloves with the fingers spread wide apart.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse wild crane's-bills with the common garden geraniums sold at nurseries - those showy, colorful flowers are actually from a different plant family entirely (Pelargonium), even though they're often just called 'geraniums' at the store.
compareHints: Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery. It's also one of the smallest species, lacking the robust growth of wild geranium or the strong smell of Herb Robert.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
